en: Itivuttaka 52 Tikanipāta, Paṭhamavagga Thus it was said by the Blessed One; having been said by the Sublime One, it was thus heard by me: “Monks, there are these three kinds of persons found existing in the world. What three? The person who is like a stone, the person who is like a water jar, and the person who is like a rain cloud. And how, monks, is one a person like a stone?

Here, monks, a certain person dwells with his mind obsessed by sensual lust, overcome by sensual lust, and he does not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen sensual lust. He dwells with his mind obsessed by ill will, overcome by ill will, and he does not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen ill will. He dwells with his mind obsessed by dullness and drowsiness, overcome by dullness and drowsiness, and he does not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen dullness and drowsiness. He dwells with his mind obsessed by restlessness and remorse, overcome by restlessness and remorse, and he does not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen restlessness and remorse. He dwells with his mind obsessed by doubt, overcome by doubt, and he does not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen doubt. Just as a stone of great size, lying on a mountain peak, would be struck by rain, wind, and heat, yet would remain as it was, so too, monks, this person dwells with his mind obsessed by these hindrances... and he does not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen doubt. This, monks, is called a person like a stone. And how, monks, is one a person like a water jar? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with his mind obsessed by sensual lust... and he does not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen doubt. But when he has emerged from that concentration, he understands as it really is the escape from the arisen doubt. Just as a water jar, full of water, placed on a stand, would be struck by rain, wind, and heat, yet would remain as it was, so too, monks, this person dwells with his mind obsessed by these hindrances... and he does not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen doubt. But when he has emerged from that concentration, he understands as it really is the escape from the arisen doubt. This, monks, is called a person like a water jar. And how, monks, is one a person like a rain cloud? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with his mind obsessed by sensual lust... and he does not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen doubt. But when he has emerged from that concentration, he understands as it really is the escape from the arisen doubt. And he applies himself to the cultivation of the path leading to the complete destruction of the taints. Just as a rain cloud, having gathered, would pour down rain upon the earth, and the water would fill the low-lying places, the middle places, and the high places, so too, monks, this person dwells with his mind obsessed by these hindrances... and he does not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen doubt. But when he has emerged from that concentration, he understands as it really is the escape from the arisen doubt. And he applies himself to the cultivation of the path leading to the complete destruction of the taints. This, monks, is called a person like a rain cloud. These, monks, are the three kinds of persons found existing in the world. Thus it was said by the Blessed One. Having said this, the Happy One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. Then, not long after the Blessed One had departed, the venerable Ānanda addressed the monks: “Friends, monks! “Yes, friend,” those monks replied to the venerable Ānanda. The venerable Ānanda said this: “Friends, the Blessed One taught these three kinds of persons. What three? The person like a stone, the person like a water jar, and the person like a rain cloud. And how, friends, is one a person like a stone?... [as above] ...This, friends, is called a person like a stone. And how, friends, is one a person like a water jar?... [as above] ...This, friends, is called a person like a water jar. And how, friends, is one a person like a rain cloud?... [as above] ...This, friends, is called a person like a rain cloud. These, friends, are the three kinds of persons taught by the Blessed One. Thus it was said by the Blessed One. Having said this, the Happy One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. And this is the meaning of what was said by the Blessed One; and so it was understood by the Venerable Ānanda. Thus have I heard.
This was said by the Blessed One, said by the Arahant; thus have I heard:
Pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling—
these, monks, are the three feelings.”
The Blessed One spoke this matter.
The mindful disciple of the Buddha understands feelings and the origin of feelings.
and the path leading to their destruction—
through the destruction of feelings, a bhikkhu [is liberated].
“Free from hunger, he has attained final Nibbāna.
This matter was also spoken by the Blessed One; thus have I heard.
